notes.text: One might take Coptic *hrosch* and Sanskrit *rôsha*, both meaning ‘anger’, to be of the same kind. The *h* might be a mere aspiration of the *r*, just as *hloili* also occurs as *loili*. Closer comparison, however, shows that *hrosch* arose from *horsch*, which has the same meaning, just as *hroyr* arose from *hoyrooy* and *heri*. The resemblance in sound to the Indian word is therefore merely accidental.

term_guide.text: A *presentation* is how an object becomes present to someone’s mind. The object can be corporeal or formed by the mind. A word gives the concept a shape from a particular standpoint, and the presentation given by the word continues to act alongside the individual’s presentation of the object. *Apprehension* names the way of taking up the object.

The sound of a word can continue across generations while its content varies. The German terms for sound overlap. In §91 *Schall* draws attention to the audible sound that may stay the same even when the word as actually thought or spoken changes.

In §90 a word’s *matter* is how it presents objects along the logical, sensory and affective lines set out in §87. Its *form* is how the faculties work together in those respects. In §89 sensory and affective content is transformed by imagination, which can preserve it as form. *Material* also names what the words provide for discourse in §72.

The *motivating meaning* is what gives a word its particular way of designating a concept. It can lie in a perceptible feature of a thing or in a metaphor. Humboldt distinguishes cases where speakers still feel the motivation from those where a historical investigator can recover it.

A sign in the strict sense designates something with an existence of its own. A concept takes its completed shape through a word. The natural form of a symbol can stand on its own, and its idea can be seen throughout that form. A word can have symbolic properties even though its sound and concept have the more tightly joined relation described in §101.

Each language makes a view of the world available through its ways of forming and designating concepts. There is room within that view for individual modes of presentation and for changes in language and thought over time.

A stem word is a starting point for an analysis of word formation. Root words can serve as stem words for derivation and composition and are constrained in connected discourse. The analysis traces relative starting points. Humboldt also rejects the forced assignment of every word to a proposed root.

The term *feeling* includes the intellectual orientation that operates without clear reflective awareness in forming and using words. §105 distinguishes particular emotions from a combined intellectual and affective disposition. *Inner life* renders *Gemüth* where its affective capacities matter.

Humboldt lists *words of possession* among families formed by a recurring procedure. He explains the basis of the class through a factual relation of possession. The passage gives no forms from which to identify a particular grammatical category.
